landings.p1: This kindergarten worksheet puts two small groups of cows, sheep and a hen on each row, with a plus sign between them and an empty box after the equals sign. Children count the animals in the first group, count the second group, and write how many there are altogether. The pictures carry the whole problem, so a child who cannot yet read an equation can still solve every row by touching and counting.
landings.p2: Counting two groups and then saying how many there are in all is the earliest form of addition. Long before the plus sign means anything, a child who can combine a pile of animals with another pile and recount the whole set is already adding. Keeping the totals within ten lets a kindergartner check the answer by counting rather than guessing.
landings.p3: On the board the whole class can count the herd together before anyone writes a number. Try addition with vehicles next, or take some away in subtraction with animals.

landings.p1: This kindergarten worksheet puts two small groups of buckets, spades and a starfish on each row, with a plus sign between them and an empty box after the equals sign. Children count the beach things in the first group, count the second group, and write how many there are altogether. The pictures carry the whole problem, so a child who cannot yet read an equation can still solve every row by touching and counting.
landings.p2: Sums are kept small, within ten, so every answer can be reached by counting the pictures rather than recalled from memory. That keeps the focus on understanding what addition does — putting two groups of beach things together — instead of racing for a fact a five-year-old has not met yet.
landings.p3: A friendly pick for a summer-theme week. Pack up camp in addition with camping gear, or count a barnyard in addition with animals.

landings.p1: This kindergarten worksheet puts two small groups of hats, belts and a scarf on each row, with a plus sign between them and an empty box after the equals sign. Children count the accessories in the first group, count the second group, and write how many there are altogether. The pictures carry the whole problem, so a child who cannot yet read an equation can still solve every row by touching and counting.
landings.p2: Each row ends with a single question — how many altogether — which quietly teaches that the last number you count is the size of the whole set. Linking the count to that total is the cardinality idea kindergartners are working out, and pictured accessories keep it something they can point at.
landings.p3: Works with a getting-dressed topic. Count a barnyard in addition with animals, or roll out in addition with vehicles.

landings.p1: Children add here by counting what they can see. Each line lays out a little set of buses, trucks and a digger, a plus sign, and a second set, with the total left blank. They count the first set, keep counting on into the second, and write how many vehicles there are in all — addition before any symbol has to be read.
landings.p2: Before written sums make sense, addition has to happen with real things a child can move and count. Joining one group of vehicles to another and finding the total builds the idea that two amounts can become one larger amount — the concrete ground that written symbols are built on later in the year.
landings.p3: Suits a child who would rather count trucks than apples. Count a barnyard in addition with animals, or work out a difference in subtraction with vehicles.
